{{Short description|Algebraic invariant}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Milnor K-theory'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Milnor|first=John|author-link=John Milnor|date=1970-12-01|title=Algebraic K -theory and quadratic forms|url=https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN356556735_0009?tify={%22pages%22:[330]}|journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]|language=en|volume=9|issue=4|pages=318–344|doi=10.1007/BF01425486|bibcode=1970InMat...9..318M|s2cid=13549621|issn=1432-1297|url-access=subscription}}</ref> is an algebraic invariant (denoted <math>K_*(F)</math> for a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>F</math>) defined by {{harvs|txt|last=Milnor|first=John|year=1970|author-link=John Milnor}} as an attempt to study higher [[algebraic K-theory]] in the special case of [[field (mathematics)|fields]]. It was hoped this would help illuminate the structure for algebraic {{nowrap|K-theory}} and give some insight about its relationships with other parts of mathematics, such as [[Galois cohomology]] and the [[Witt group#Grothendieck-Witt ring|Grothendieck–Witt ring]] of [[quadratic form]]s. Before Milnor K-theory was defined, there existed ad-hoc definitions for <math>K_1</math> and <math>K_2</math>. Fortunately, it can be shown Milnor {{nowrap|K-theory}} is a part of algebraic {{nowrap|K-theory}}, which in general is the easiest part to compute.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Totaro|first=Burt|author-link=Burt Totaro|title=Milnor K-Theory is the Simplest Part of Algebraic K-Theory|url=https://www.math.ucla.edu/~totaro/papers/public_html/milnor.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202192833/https://www.math.ucla.edu/~totaro/papers/public_html/milnor.pdf|archive-date=2 Dec 2020}}</ref>

==Definition==

=== Motivation ===
After the definition of the [[Grothendieck group#Example: The Grothendieck group of a ring|Grothendieck group]] <math>K(R)</math> of a [[commutative ring]], it was expected there should be a sequence of invariants <math>K_i(R)</math> called higher {{nowrap|K-theory}} groups, from the fact that there exists a [[short exact sequence]]
:<math>K(R,I) \to K(R) \to K(R/I) \to 0</math>
which should have a continuation by a [[long exact sequence]]. Note the group on the left is relative {{nowrap|K-theory}}. This led to much study and as a first guess for what this theory would look like, Milnor gave a definition for fields. His definition is based upon two calculations of what higher {{nowrap|K-theory}} "should" look like in degrees <math>1</math> and <math>2</math>. Then, if in a later generalization of algebraic {{nowrap|K-theory}} was given, if the generators of <math>K_*(R)</math> lived in degree <math>1</math> and the relations in degree <math>2</math>, then the constructions in degrees <math>1</math> and <math>2</math> would give the structure for the rest of the {{nowrap|K-theory}} ring. Under this assumption, Milnor gave his "ad-hoc" definition. It turns out algebraic {{nowrap|K-theory}} <math>K_*(R)</math> in general has a more complex structure, but for fields the Milnor {{nowrap|K-theory}} groups are contained in the general algebraic {{nowrap|K-theory}} groups after tensoring with <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>, i.e. <math>K^M_n(F)\otimes \mathbb{Q} \subseteq K_n(F)\otimes \mathbb{Q}</math>.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|date=1981-01-01|title=Relations between the milnor and quillen K-theory of fields|journal=Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra|language=en|volume=20|issue=1|pages=93–102|doi=10.1016/0022-4049(81)90051-7|issn=0022-4049|last1=Shapiro|first1=Jack M.|doi-access=free}}</ref> It turns out the natural map <math>\lambda:K^M_4(F) \to K_4(F)</math> fails to be injective for a [[global field]] <math>F</math><ref name=":2" /><sup>pg 96</sup>.

=== Definition ===
Note for fields the Grothendieck group can be readily computed as <math>K_0(F) = \mathbb{Z}</math> since the only [[finitely generated module]]s are finite-[[dimension (vector space)|dimensional]] [[vector space]]s. Also, Milnor's definition of higher {{nowrap|K-groups}} depends upon the canonical [[isomorphism]]
:<math>l\colon K_1(F) \to F^*</math>
(the [[group of units]] of <math>F</math>) and observing the [[Matsumoto's theorem (K-theory)|calculation of ''K''<sub>2</sub> of a field]] by [[Hideya Matsumoto]], which gave the simple presentation
:<math>K_2(F) = \frac{F^*\otimes F^*}{\{l(a)\otimes l(1-a) : a \neq 0 ,1\}}</math>
for a two-sided ideal generated by elements <math>l(a)\otimes l(a-1)</math>, called [[Steinberg group (K-theory)|Steinberg relations]]. Milnor took the hypothesis that these were the only relations, hence he gave the following "ad-hoc" definition of '''Milnor K-theory''' as
:<math>K_n^M(F) = \frac{K_1(F)\otimes \cdots \otimes K_1(F)}{\{l(a_1)\otimes \cdots \otimes l(a_n) : a_i + a_{i+1} = 1 \}}.</math>
The direct sum of these groups is isomorphic to a [[tensor algebra]] over the integers of the [[multiplicative group]] <math>K_1(F) \cong F^*</math> modded out by the [[two-sided ideal]] generated by:
:<math>\left \{ l(a)\otimes l(1-a) : 0,1 \neq a \in F \right \}</math>
so
:<math>\bigoplus_{n=0}^\infty K_n^M(F) \cong \frac{T^*(K_1^M(F))}{\{l(a)\otimes l(1-a) : a \neq 0,1\}}</math>
showing his definition is a direct extension of the Steinberg relations.

== Properties ==

=== Ring structure ===
The graded module <math>K_*^M(F)</math> is a [[supercommutative algebra|graded-commutative]] ring<ref name=":0" /><sup>pg 1-3</sup>.<ref name="GS184">Gille & Szamuely (2006), p.&nbsp;184.</ref> If we write
:<math>(l(a_1)\otimes\cdots \otimes l(a_n))\cdot
(l(b_1)\otimes\cdots \otimes l(b_m))</math>
as
:<math>l(a_1)\otimes\cdots \otimes l(a_n) \otimes l(b_1)\otimes\cdots \otimes l(b_m)</math>
then for <math>\xi \in K_i^M(F)</math> and <math>\eta \in K^M_j(F)</math> we have
:<math>\xi \cdot \eta = (-1)^{i \cdot j}\eta \cdot \xi.</math>
From the [[mathematical proof|proof]] of this property, there are some additional properties which fall out, like <math display="block">l(a)^2 = l(a)l(-1)</math> for <math>l(a) \in K_1(F)</math> since <math>l(a)l(-a) = 0</math>. Also, if <math>a_1+\cdots + a_n</math> of non-zero fields elements equals <math>0,1</math>, then <math display="block">l(a_1)\cdots l(a_n) = 0</math> There's a direct arithmetic application: <math>-1 \in F</math> is a sum of squares [[if and only if]] every positive dimensional <math>K_n^M(F)</math> is nilpotent, which is a powerful statement about the structure of Milnor {{nowrap|K-groups}}. In particular, for the fields <math>\mathbb{Q}(i)</math>, <math>\mathbb{Q}_p(i)</math> with <math>\sqrt{-1} \not\in \mathbb{Q}_p</math>, all of its Milnor {{nowrap|K-groups}} are nilpotent. In the converse case, the field <math>F</math> can be embedded into a [[real closed field]], which gives a total ordering on the field.

=== Relation to Higher Chow groups and Quillen's higher K-theory ===
One of the core properties relating Milnor K-theory to higher algebraic K-theory is the fact there exists natural isomorphisms <math display="block">K_n^M(F) \to \text{CH}^{n}(F,n)</math> to Bloch's [[Bloch's higher Chow group|Higher chow groups]] which induces a morphism of graded rings <math display="block">K_*^M(F) \to \text{CH}^*(F,*)</math> This can be verified using an explicit morphism<ref name=":1" /><sup>pg 181</sup> <math display="block">\phi:F^* \to \text{CH}^1(F,1)</math> where <math display="block">\phi(a)\phi(1-a) = 0 ~\text{in}~ \text{CH}^2(F,2) ~\text{for}~ a,1-a \in F^*</math> This map is given by <math display="block">\begin{align}
\{1\} &\mapsto 0 \in \text{CH}^1(F,1) \\
\{a\} &\mapsto [a] \in \text{CH}^1(F,1)
\end{align}</math> for <math>[a]</math> the class of the point <math>[a:1] \in \mathbb{P}^1_F-\{0,1,\infty \}</math> with <math>a \in F^*-\{1\}</math>. The main property to check is that <math>[a] + [1/a] = 0</math> for <math>a \in F^*-\{1\}</math> and <math>[a] + [b] = [ab]</math>. Note this is distinct from <math>[a]\cdot [b]</math> since this is an element in <math>\text{CH}^2(F,2)</math>. Also, the second property implies the first for <math>b = 1/a</math>. This check can be done using a rational curve defining a cycle in <math>C^1(F,2)</math> whose image under the boundary map <math>\partial</math> is the sum <math>[a] + [b] - [ab]</math>for <math>ab \neq 1</math>, showing they differ by a boundary. Similarly, if <math>ab=1</math> the boundary map sends this cycle to <math>[a] - [1/a]</math>, showing they differ by a boundary.
The second main property to show is the Steinberg relations. With these, and the fact the higher Chow groups have a ring structure <math display="block">\text{CH}^p(F,q) \otimes \text{CH}^r(F,s) \to \text{CH}^{p+r}(F,q+s)</math> we get an explicit map <math display="block">K_*^M(F) \to \text{CH}^*(F,*)</math> Showing the map in the reverse direction is an isomorphism is more work, but we get the isomorphisms <math display="block">K_n^M(F) \to \text{CH}^n(F,n)</math> We can then relate the higher Chow groups to higher algebraic K-theory using the fact there are isomorphisms <math display="block">K_n(X)\otimes \mathbb{Q} \cong \bigoplus_p \text{CH}^p(X,n)\otimes \mathbb{Q}</math> giving the relation to Quillen's higher algebraic K-theory. Note that the maps
:<math>K^M_n(F) \to K_n(F)</math>

from the Milnor K-groups of a field to the [[Daniel Quillen|Quillen]] K-groups, which is an isomorphism for <math>n\le 2</math> but not for larger ''n'', in general. For nonzero elements <math>a_1, \ldots, a_n</math> in ''F'', the '''symbol''' <math>\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}</math> in <math>K_n^M(F)</math> means the image of <math>a_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes a_n</math> in the tensor algebra. Every element of Milnor K-theory can be written as a finite sum of symbols. The fact that <math>\{a, 1-a\} = 0</math> in <math>K_2^M(F)</math> for <math>a \in F\setminus \{0,1\}</math> is sometimes called the '''Steinberg relation'''.

=== Representation in motivic cohomology ===
In [[motivic cohomology]], specifically [[motivic homotopy theory]], there is a [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]] <math>K_{n,A}</math> representing a generalization of Milnor K-theory with coefficients in an [[abelian group]] <math>A</math>. If we denote <math>A_{tr}(X) = \mathbb{Z}_{tr}(X)\otimes A</math> then we define the sheaf <math>K_{n,A}</math> as the sheafification of the following pre-sheaf<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Voevodsky|first=Vladimir|date=2001-07-15|title=Reduced power operations in motivic cohomology|eprint=math/0107109 }}</ref><sup>pg 4</sup> <math display="block">K_{n,A}^{pre}: U \mapsto A_{tr}(\mathbb{A}^n)(U)/A_{tr}(\mathbb{A}^n - \{0\})(U)</math> Note that sections of this pre-sheaf are equivalent classes of cycles on <math>U\times\mathbb{A}^n</math> with coefficients in <math>A</math> which are equidimensional and finite over <math>U</math> (which follows straight from the definition of <math>\mathbb{Z}_{tr}(X)</math>). It can be shown there is an <math>\mathbb{A}^1</math>-weak equivalence with the motivic Eilenberg-Maclane sheaves <math>K(A, 2n,n)</math> (depending on the grading convention).

==Examples==

=== Finite fields ===
For a [[finite field]] <math>F = \mathbb{F}_q</math>, <math>K_1^M(F)</math> is a cyclic group of order <math>q-1</math> (since is it isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{F}_q^*</math>), so graded commutativity gives <math display="block"> l(a)\cdot l(b) = -l(b)\cdot l(a)</math> hence <math display="block"> l(a)^2 =-l(a) ^2</math> Because <math>K_2^M(F)</math> is a [[finite group]], this implies it must have order <math>\leq 2</math>. Looking further, <math>1</math> can always be expressed as a sum of quadratic non-residues, i.e. elements <math>a,b \in F</math> such that <math>[a],[b] \in F/F^{\times 2}</math> are not equal to <math>0</math>, hence <math>a + b = 1</math> showing <math>K_2^M(F) = 0</math>. Because the Steinberg relations generate all relations in the Milnor K-theory ring, we have <math>K_n^M(F) = 0</math> for <math>n > 2</math>.

=== Real numbers ===
For the field of [[real number]]s <math>\mathbb{R}</math> the Milnor {{nowrap|K-theory}} groups can be readily computed. In degree <math>n</math> the group is generated by <math display="block"> K_n^M(\mathbb{R}) = \{(-1)^n, l(a_1)\cdots l(a_n) : a_1,\ldots, a_n > 0 \}</math> where <math>(-1)^n</math> gives a group of order <math>2</math> and the subgroup generated by the <math>l(a_1)\cdots l(a_n)</math> is divisible. The subgroup generated by <math>(-1)^n</math> is not divisible because otherwise it could be expressed as a sum of squares. The Milnor K-theory ring is important in the study of motivic homotopy theory because it gives generators for part of the motivic [[Steenrod algebra]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bachmann|first=Tom|date=May 2018|title=Motivic and Real Etale Stable Homotopy Theory|journal=Compositio Mathematica|volume=154|issue=5|pages=883–917|doi=10.1112/S0010437X17007710|issn=0010-437X|arxiv=1608.08855|s2cid=119305101}}</ref> The others are lifts from the classical Steenrod operations to motivic cohomology.

=== Other calculations ===
<math>K^M_2(\Complex)</math> is an [[uncountable set|uncountable]] uniquely [[divisible group]].<ref>An abelian group is '''uniquely divisible''' if it is a vector space over the [[rational number]]s.</ref> Also, <math>K^M_2(\R)</math> is the [[direct sum]] of a [[cyclic group]] of [[order (group theory)|order]] 2 and an uncountable uniquely divisible group; <math>K^M_2(\Q_p)</math> is the direct sum of the multiplicative group of <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> and an uncountable uniquely divisible group; <math>K^M_2(\Q)</math> is the direct sum of the cyclic group of order 2 and cyclic groups of order <math>p-1</math> for all odd prime <math>p</math>. For <math>n \geq 3</math>, <math>K_n^M(\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2</math>. The full proof is in the appendix of Milnor's original paper.<ref name=":0" /> Some of the computation can be seen by looking at a map on <math>K_2^M(F)</math> induced from the inclusion of a global field <math>F</math> to its completions <math>F_v</math>, so there is a morphism<math display="block"> K_2^M(F) \to \bigoplus_{v} K_2^M(F_v)/(\text{max. divis. subgr.})</math> whose kernel finitely generated. In addition, the [[cokernel]] is isomorphic to the [[roots of unity]] in <math>F</math>.

In addition, for a general local field <math>F</math> (such as a finite extension <math>K/\mathbb{Q}_p</math>), the Milnor {{nowrap|K-groups}} <math>K_n^M(F)</math> are divisible.

=== K<sub>*</sub><sup>M</sup>(F(t)) ===
There is a general structure theorem computing <math>K_n^M(F(t))</math> for a field <math>F</math> in relation to the Milnor {{nowrap|K-theory}} of <math>F</math> and extensions <math>F[t]/(\pi)</math> for non-zero primes ideals <math>(\pi) \in \text{Spec}(F[t])</math>. This is given by an exact sequence <math display="block"> 0 \to K_n^M(F) \to K_n^M(F(t)) \xrightarrow{\partial_\pi} \bigoplus_{(\pi) \in \text{Spec}(F[t])} K_{n-1}F[t]/(\pi) \to 0</math> where <math>\partial_\pi : K_n^M(F(t)) \to K_{n-1}F[t]/(\pi)</math> is a morphism constructed from a reduction of <math>F</math> to <math>\overline{F}_v</math> for a discrete valuation <math>v</math>. This follows from the theorem there exists only one homomorphism <math display="block"> \partial:K_n^M(F) \to K_{n-1}^M(\overline{F})</math> which for the group of units <math>U \subset F</math> which are elements have valuation <math>0</math>, having a natural morphism <math display="block"> U \to \overline{F}_v^*</math> where <math>u \mapsto \overline{u}</math> we have <math display="block"> \partial(l(\pi)l(u_2)\cdots l(u_n)) = l(\overline{u}_2)\cdots  l(\overline{u}_n)</math> where <math>\pi</math> a [[prime element]], meaning <math>\text{Ord}_v(\pi) = 1</math>, and <math display="block"> \partial(l(u_1)\cdots l(u_n)) = 0</math> Since every non-zero [[prime ideal]] <math>(\pi) \in \text{Spec}(F[t])</math> gives a valuation <math>v_\pi : F(t) \to F[t]/(\pi)</math>, we get the map <math>\partial_\pi</math> on the Milnor K-groups.

==Applications==
Milnor K-theory plays a fundamental role in [[Higher local field#Class field theory|higher class field theory]], replacing <math>K_1^M(F) = F^{\times}\!</math> in the one-dimensional [[class field theory]].

Milnor K-theory fits into the broader context of [[motivic cohomology]], via the isomorphism

:<math>K^M_n(F) \cong H^n(F, \Z(n))</math>

of the Milnor K-theory of a field with a certain motivic cohomology group.<ref>Mazza, Voevodsky, Weibel (2005), Theorem 5.1.</ref> In this sense, the apparently ad hoc definition of Milnor {{nowrap|K-theory}} becomes a theorem: certain motivic cohomology groups of a field can be explicitly computed by [[generators and relations]].

A much deeper result, the [[norm residue isomorphism theorem|Bloch-Kato conjecture]] (also called the norm residue isomorphism theorem), relates Milnor {{nowrap|K-theory}} to [[Galois cohomology]] or [[étale cohomology]]:

:<math>K^M_n(F)/r \cong H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(F, \Z/r(n)),</math>

for any positive integer ''r'' invertible in the field ''F''. This conjecture was proved by [[Vladimir Voevodsky]], with contributions by [[Markus Rost]] and others.<ref>Voevodsky (2011).</ref> This includes the theorem of [[Alexander Merkurjev]] and [[Andrei Suslin]] as well as the [[Milnor conjecture (K-theory)|Milnor conjecture]] as special cases (the cases when <math>n = 2</math> and <math>r = 2</math>, respectively).

Finally, there is a relation between Milnor K-theory and [[quadratic form]]s. For a field ''F'' of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] not 2, define the fundamental ideal ''I'' in the [[Witt ring (forms)|Witt ring]] of quadratic forms over ''F'' to be the kernel of the homomorphism <math>W(F) \to\Z/2</math> given by the dimension of a quadratic form, modulo 2. Milnor defined a homomorphism:

:<math>\begin{cases} K_n^M(F)/2 \to I^n/I^{n+1} \\ \{a_1, \ldots, a_n \} \mapsto \langle \langle a_1, \ldots , a_n \rangle \rangle = \langle 1, -a_1 \rangle \otimes \cdots \otimes \langle 1, -a_n \rangle \end{cases}</math>

where <math>\langle \langle a_1, a_2, \ldots , a_n \rangle \rangle</math> denotes the class of the ''n''-fold [[Pfister form]].<ref>Elman, Karpenko, Merkurjev (2008), sections 5 and 9.B.</ref>

Dmitri Orlov, Alexander Vishik, and Voevodsky proved another statement called the Milnor conjecture, namely that this homomorphism <math>K_n^M(F)/2 \to I^n/I^{n+1}</math> is an isomorphism.<ref>Orlov, Vishik, Voevodsky (2007).</ref>
